title: Estimating pitch with autocorrelation, and what ASR is
summary: Explain why pitch is not 1 / frame length; compute a dot product and an autocorrelation by hand and read the period off the first peak; turn a lag in samples into F0 = Fₛ / lag; say which heuristics (pitch range, silence, voicing) throw out bad frames; lay out the ASR pipeline and compute word error rate.
sourceNote: Dr. Koo's Day 9 slides 'Pitch estimation' and Day 10 slides 'Overview of ASR' (pulled from Canvas); Bäckström et al. 2022 §3.7 and ch. 8.3; J&M ch. 16.1 and 16.5. Labs 8 and 9.

blocks.md: **The problem** Your voice has a pitch: how high or low it sounds. That pitch comes from how fast your vocal folds vibrate, the **fundamental frequency F0**. We want a number for it, frame by frame, across a recording. Intonation (questions going up), tone in Mandarin or Yoruba, stress, emotion and speaker identity all live in the F0 track.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this** Auto-Tune and every pitch-correction app, the pitch track in Praat, voice assistants deciding whether you asked a question, Mandarin speech recognizers telling *mā* from *mà*, and forensic speaker comparison. All of them start with exactly the method in this chapter or its cepstral cousin (Days 11–12).

Koo opens with a trick question. Isn't pitch just F0? **Yes**: pitch tracks the F0 of the source (the vocal folds). But **not** the F0 you get from the DFT's point of view. When the STFT treats a frame as one period of a repeating signal, the 'fundamental' of the DFT grid is 1 / frame length: a 0.05 s frame gives 1 / 0.05 = **20 Hz**. That number describes the frame, not the voice.

rows: how often the waveform actually repeats
a man ~ 100 Hz, a woman ~ 200 Hz
blocks.title: Don't mix these up

blocks.body: Answering 'F0 = 1 / frame size' when asked for the pitch of a frame. That's the DFT bin spacing (Day 7). Pitch has to be measured from the signal: autocorrelation or cepstrum.

sections.heading: Dot product: a number for 'same trend'

blocks.body: A number for how similar the **trend** of two equally long lists of values is: do they go up and down together?
Multiply the two lists position by position and add: `x · y = Σ xᵢ yᵢ`. Large and positive when they move together, near zero when unrelated, negative when one goes up as the other goes down.

blocks.prompt: x = [3, 0, −3], y = [1, 0, −1]. What is x · y, and what does its sign say?
blocks.answer: 3·1 + 0·0 + (−3)(−1) = 6. Positive: the two go up and down together.

sections.heading: Autocorrelation: compare the signal with itself, shifted

blocks.body: The dot product of a signal with a **delayed copy of itself**, computed for many delays (lags) k: `r[k] = Σ x[n] · x[n − k]`. The delayed copy is **padded with zeros** so both lists stay the same length.

blocks.md: Why this finds the period: if a signal repeats every T₀ samples, then shifting it by exactly T₀ lines every peak up with the next peak. The dot product jumps. Shifting by half a period lines peaks up with troughs and the dot product goes negative. So **the first peak after lag 0 is the period**.

blocks.title: Autocorrelation of a signal with period 8

frames.caption: Lag 0: the signal against itself, unshifted. Every product is a square, so this is the biggest the dot product can ever be.

lines: lag 2: x[n]·x[n−2], padded with 0s at the front
frames.caption: Shift by 2 samples: now peaks line up with zero-crossings. Products cancel out, the sum is small: 1.

lines: lag 4: shifted by half a cycle
frames.caption: Half a cycle: every peak now sits on a trough. Positive × negative everywhere: strongly negative.

lines: lag 8: shifted by one full cycle
frames.caption: One full cycle (8 samples): peaks line up with peaks again, so the dot product is large and positive again. That lag is the period.

lines: first peak after 0 is at k = 8 → period = 8 samples
frames.caption: Read the peak, not the whole list: the first peak after lag 0 is the fundamental period T₀ in samples. It's smaller than 18 only because the shifted copy was padded with zeros (fewer products to add up).

blocks.md: Two things on Koo's plot: peaks **recur** at every multiple of the period (8, 16, 24…), and they **shrink** as the lag grows, because more of the shifted copy is zero padding. Always take the first peak after 0.

blocks.body: Taking the lag-0 value as the peak. r[0] is always the largest (the signal matched with itself); it tells you nothing about pitch. Skip it and look for the next peak.

sections.heading: From a lag in samples to F0 in Hz

blocks.title: The conversion
blocks.body:
F0 = sampling rate ÷ period in samples

Koo's first example: one cycle every 99 samples at 10,000 Hz
  F0 = 10,000 ÷ 99 ≈ 101 Hz

'The emperor had a mean temper' at 16,000 Hz, a periodic frame:
  first peak at lag 69 → F0 = 16,000 ÷ 69 ≈ 232 Hz (the slide rounds to 231)

blocks.md: Read the units out loud and it can't go wrong: *(1 cycle / 99 samples) × (10,000 samples / 1 second) = 10,000 / 99 cycles per second*.

blocks.prompt: At Fₛ = 16,000 Hz the first autocorrelation peak is at lag 80. What is F0?

blocks.md: On an **aperiodic** frame (a hiss like *s*, or silence) there is no real period, but autocorrelation still has a 'first peak'. Koo's example lands at lag 6: 16,000 ÷ 6 ≈ **2,667 Hz**, which no human voice produces. So real pitch trackers throw frames out.

rows: the 2,667 Hz nonsense; at 16 kHz that means lags 27 to 213
skip the frame if no amplitude is above 3% of the recording's maximum
skip if the spectrum is too flat (spectral flatness above a threshold)
noise and voiceless sounds: speech spectra have energy peaks, noise doesn't
blocks.title: Throwing out bad frames

blocks.prompt: With a 75–600 Hz pitch range at Fₛ = 16,000 Hz, which lags are you allowed to pick?
blocks.answer: From 16,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 27 samples up to 16,000 ÷ 75 ≈ 213 samples. (High pitch = short lag.)

blocks.body: Getting a computer to take dictation: a recording goes in, a sequence of words (or phonemes) comes out.

rows: input: one spectrum vector per short frame; output: a sequence of phonemes or words; the link: HMMs or neural networks
set hyperparameters, fit on training, check on validation, repeat

blocks.slide: How an ASR system is built

blocks.md: That 'one vector per frame' input is where this course has been heading: the STFT gives you a spectrum per frame (Day 8), and Days 11–12 turn each spectrum into the compact 39-number vector that classic ASR systems actually use.

rows: read speech, hand-labelled down to phoneme and word boundaries
1,000 hours of read audiobooks, transcribed by sentence
260 hours of phone calls between strangers (conversational)
blocks.title: Standard corpora

blocks.body: Errors in the computer's output (the **hypothesis**) divided by the number of words in the true transcript (the **reference**). Errors are **substitutions** (wrong word), **deletions** (missed word) and **insertions** (extra word): `WER = (S + D + I) ÷ N`.

blocks.title: Counting WER
blocks.body:
reference:  the cat sat on the mat        (N = 6)
hypothesis: the cat sat in a the mat

'on' → 'in'   substitution  S = 1
'a'           inserted      I = 1
nothing missed               D = 0

WER = (1 + 0 + 1) ÷ 6 = 2/6 ≈ 33%

blocks.md: With several recordings, add up all the errors and all the reference words first, then divide once (Koo's slide). Don't average the per-recording percentages.

blocks.body: Dividing by the length of the hypothesis. WER always divides by the **reference** length. Because insertions count, WER can go above 100%.

blocks.prompt: Two recordings: 3 errors in a 10-word reference, 1 error in a 30-word reference. What is the overall WER?

exercises.title: Read a pitch off an autocorrelation
exercises.prompt: A frame sampled at 22,050 Hz has autocorrelation peaks at lags 0, 147, 294 and 441 (and smaller values in between). What is F0? Is it plausible for a human voice?
hints: The first peak after 0 is the period in samples.
F0 = Fₛ ÷ that lag. Then check 75–600 Hz.
solution: Inside 75–600 Hz: plausible (a lower voice). 294 and 441 are just multiples of the period.
exercises.why: This is the whole of Lab 8's pitch tracker, done by hand for one frame.

exercises.title: Count the errors
exercises.prompt: Reference: 'please call stella ask her to bring these things'. Hypothesis: 'please call stellar ask to bring these thing with'. What is the WER?
hints: Line the two up word by word. N is the reference length: count it.
'stella' → 'stellar' and 'things' → 'thing' are substitutions. Which reference word is missing?
'with' at the end is extra: an insertion.
exercises.why: WER is the one number every ASR paper, product launch and benchmark reports; knowing it divides by the reference and counts insertions keeps you from misreading them.
